claims.text: The initial equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy contains local chemical short-range-order clusters.
The initial alloy contains no pre-existing vacancy clusters.
The initial alloy contains no HCP precipitates.
Shockley partial dislocations preferentially nucleate at SRO clusters rather than at vacancy clusters.
SRO clusters generate heterogeneous lattice-strain fields.
The strain fields associated with SRO reduce the local stacking-fault-energy barrier for Shockley-partial nucleation.
Atomic-size or lattice-parameter mismatch produces lattice friction that hinders partial-dislocation motion in the HEA.
The combination of lattice friction and SRO creates energy minima for partial-dislocation nucleation.
The <11-1> loading orientation requires a higher resolved shear stress to activate slip than the <110> orientation.
The <110> orientation aligns with the slip direction and therefore permits easier partial-dislocation glide.
The <11-1>-oriented sample will have approximately 15–20% higher yield stress than the <110>-oriented sample.
The observed HCP-like regions are transient intrinsic stacking faults rather than a thermodynamic HCP phase transformation.
SRO-induced reduction of stacking-fault energy stabilizes the transient HCP-like regions.
HCP-like regions caused by stacking faults will revert to FCC during unloading or annealing.
A true phase-transformed HCP region would persist during unloading or require substantially more energy to reverse.
A chemically random FCC FeNiCrMn single crystal has no orientation dependence of yield stress and is mechanically isotropic.
In the chemically random baseline, dislocations nucleate randomly at free surfaces.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis concerns Shockley partial dislocations, but the mechanism identifies the operative system as {111}<110> and describes <110> as the partial-glide direction. In FCC crystals, <110> denotes the conventional perfect-dislocation slip direction, whereas Shockley partials have <112>-type Burgers vectors.

The baseline assumes no orientation dependence and isotropic yield in a random FCC single crystal, while the mechanism attributes a large orientation dependence to resolved-shear geometry. Removing SRO does not by itself remove crystallographic orientation dependence.

The boundary explicitly excludes refractory BCC HEAs, yet the proposed SRO–dislocation mechanism is partly motivated by evidence from BCC MoNbTaW and SRO-clustering evidence from refractory HfNbTaTiZr without explaining why those mechanisms transfer to FCC FeNiCrMn.
